metadata.description: Canonical CS ontology entries for operating system concepts taught in undergraduate CS courses.
sources: Operating System Concepts – Silberschatz et al.

entries.label: OS_CONCEPT
entries.definition: The process of saving and restoring the state of a CPU so that multiple processes can share a single CPU resource.

entries.label: OS_CONCEPT
entries.definition: An instance of a program in execution, consisting of code, data, stack, and OS resources.

entries.label: OS_CONCEPT
entries.definition: The smallest unit of CPU execution within a process; multiple threads share the process's memory space.

entries.label: OS_CONCEPT
entries.definition: The ability of a CPU or a single process to execute multiple threads concurrently.

entries.label: OS_CONCEPT
entries.definition: A synchronisation primitive that grants exclusive access to a shared resource to only one thread at a time.

entries.label: OS_CONCEPT
entries.definition: A synchronisation variable used to control access to a common resource by multiple processes.

entries.label: OS_CONCEPT
entries.definition: A state where two or more processes are each waiting for the other to release a resource, resulting in indefinite blocking.

entries.label: OS_CONCEPT
entries.definition: A memory management technique that gives processes the illusion of having more memory than is physically available.

entries.label: OS_CONCEPT
entries.definition: A memory management scheme that eliminates contiguous physical memory by dividing memory into fixed-size pages.

entries.label: OS_CONCEPT
entries.definition: A memory management scheme that divides memory into variable-size segments corresponding to logical units.

entries.label: OS_CONCEPT
entries.definition: An exception raised when a process accesses a memory page that is not currently in physical RAM.

entries.label: OS_CONCEPT
entries.definition: A condition where excessive paging activity causes poor system performance because the OS spends more time paging than executing.

entries.label: OS_CONCEPT
entries.definition: The period of time for which a process is allowed to run in a preemptive multitasking system.

entries.label: OS_CONCEPT
entries.definition: A signal to the processor that requires immediate attention, causing the CPU to suspend current execution.

entries.label: OS_CONCEPT
entries.definition: A programmatic interface through which user programs request services from the OS kernel.

entries.label: OS_CONCEPT
entries.definition: A CPU scheduling algorithm where each process is assigned a fixed time slice in cyclic order.

entries.label: OS_CONCEPT
entries.definition: A CPU scheduling algorithm that selects the process with the smallest execution time next.

entries.label: OS_CONCEPT
entries.definition: A CPU scheduling algorithm that assigns the CPU to processes in the order they arrive.

entries.label: OS_CONCEPT
entries.definition: Mechanisms that allow processes to communicate with each other and synchronise actions.

entries.label: OS_CONCEPT
entries.definition: A bug where the outcome of a program depends on the non-deterministic order of thread execution.

entries.label: OS_CONCEPT
entries.definition: A section of code that accesses shared resources and must not be executed by more than one thread at a time.

entries.label: OS_CONCEPT
entries.definition: The central component of an operating system that manages CPU, memory, and device drivers.

entries.label: OS_CONCEPT
entries.definition: A user interface for accessing OS services, either command-line (CLI) or graphical (GUI).

entries.label: OS_CONCEPT
entries.definition: A system call that creates a new process (child) as a copy of the calling process (parent).

entries.label: OS_CONCEPT
entries.definition: A unidirectional data channel used for IPC between a writing process and a reading process.

entries.label: OS_CONCEPT
entries.definition: The OS component that selects which process runs on the CPU at any given time.

entries.label: OS_CONCEPT
entries.definition: The OS module that gives control of the CPU to the process selected by the scheduler.
